S) and self-transcendence (ESSS) followed the same order: highest for transformative, then amazement, then reverential awe experiences (AWE-S: F(2, 209.38) = 17.84, p < .001; ESSS: F(2, 202.43) = 11.16, p < .001; all pairwise ps ≤ .010).

Our pre-registered predictions for the AWE-S subscales and self-diffidence were partly supported (see SM.3). As expected, perceived vastness was higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences (0.39 SD, p < .001). Need for accommodation was highest for transformative awe experiences, although this difference was significant only compared with reverential awe experiences.

Contrary to our predictions, self-diminishment and self-diffidence were higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences, and connectedness was higher rather than equal. Finally, the awe measures were positively correlated across experiences, with the exception of reverence ratings (see SM.3). As predicted, participants rarely rated their awe experiences as religious, but often rated them as spiritual. Of the 320 experiences (145 participants), 90.0% were rated as not at all religious (0), and none received the highest rating (4). In contrast, 52.5% were rated as at least somewhat spiritual. At the participant level, 13.1% of participants rated at least one of their experiences as religious, and 58.6% rated at least one as spiritual.

Spiritual ratings were higher than religious ratings for all three types of awe. However, the size of the difference depended on the type, Item × Type: F(2, 500.16) = 6.35, p = .002 (see SM.3 for model details). The difference was -1.44 for transformative, -0.89 for amazement and -0.77 for reverential awe experiences (all ps < .001). Transformative awe experiences were rated as spiritual more often (77.8%) than amazement (48.6%) and reverential awe experiences (48.0%). Religious ratings did not differ between types.

As predicted, spiritual ratings increased with the extent of awe. They were associated with AWE-S (β = .41), ESSS (β = .36) and awe ladder scores (β = .26; all ps < .001), and less strongly with amazement ratings (β = .13, p = .005). They were not associated with reverence ratings (β = .02, p = .622). Religious ratings were weakly associated with AWE-S (β = .14, p = .009) and ESSS scores (β = .13, p = .014), but not with the other awe measures (ps ≥ .121; Table SM.3.2).

Outcomes of awe experiences

Descriptives

First, we examined the pre-and post scores of our core variables, and investigated if these changed significantly; see Table 3. Note. Paired-samples t tests. After Holm correction across the five comparisons, the decreases in spiritual yearning (p = .002) and wellbeing (p = .04) remained significant (other ps ≥ .34).

Frequency of awe and outcomes

To test whether more frequent awe experiences were associated with greater outcomes (Hypothesis 3a), we computed a frequency index. Each participant's frequency ratings (0 = none,1 = once,2 = two or three times,3 = more than three times) were summed across the three types of awe and both diary entries (range 0-18). Frequency was not associated with post-summer meaning in life (β = .07, p = .15), wellbeing (β = .03, p = .57) or spirituality (β = .02, p = .73) after accounting for pre-summer scores. It was associated with post-summer spiritual yearning (β = .12, p = .04, ΔR² = .013). However, this association did not remain once the AWE-S scores were added (β = .05; Step 3: ΔR² = .008, p = .46). Pre-summer scores accounted for most of the variance in all outcomes (βs = 72-.84; Table SM.5.1).

As a robustness check, we repeated the cumulative models using change scores (post-summer minus pre-summer) as outcomes (n = 127). None of the sets of predictors were associated with change in any outcome (see SM.5).

Extent of awe and outcomes

To test whether a greater extent of awe was associated with greater outcomes (Hypotheses 3a and 3c summer scores accounted for most of the variance in all outcomes (βs = .64-.83 in the final models;

Table SM.6.1).

Spiritual yearning

We pre-registered that awe experiences would increase spiritual yearning in participants with low presummer scores and decrease it in those with high pre-summer scores. To test this, we added the interaction between pre-summer spiritual yearning and awe to regression models predicting postsummer spiritual yearning. The awe predictors were frequency, overall AWE-S, and AWE-S for each type of awe, and all variables were standardised (n = 154 for frequency and n = 160 for the AWE-S scores). None of the interactions were significant: frequency, β = -.01, p = .83; overall AWE-S, β = -.05, p = .33; transformative awe, β = -.10, p = .06; amazement awe, β = -.04, p = .49; reverential awe, β = -.03, p = .58. The hypothesis was therefore not supported (Supplementary Materials).

Peak experiences

The following analyses were not pre-registered. We examined whether participants' peak experience, which was their most awe-inspiring experience of the summer (see Method), predicted the outcomes (n = 131). For each outcome, we ran hierarchical regressions with standardised variables. Model 1 included the pre-summer score and the number of rated awe experiences (1-6). Model 2 added the amazement and reverence ratings of the peak experience. Model 3 added the six AWE-S subscale scores of the peak experience (time perception, self-diminishment, connectedness, vastness, physical sensations, and need for accommodation). The number of rated awe experiences was not associated with any of the outcomes.

The awe ratings of the peak experience explained additional variance in post-summer meaning in life, ΔR² = .021, F(2, 126) = 4.75, p = .01. They also explained additional variance in post-summer wellbeing, ΔR² = .040, F(2, 126) = 6.71, p = .002. In both cases, the amazement rating predicted higher scores (meaning in life: β = .12, p = .01; wellbeing: β = .19, p < .001), whereas the reverence rating did not (ps ≥ .11). The AWE-S subscales did not explain further variance in meaning in life or wellbeing (ΔR²s ≤ .013, ps ≥ .64). Neither set of predictors explained additional variance in spiritual yearning or spirituality (ΔR²s ≤ .038, ps ≥ .14). Pre-summer scores accounted for most of the variance in all outcomes (Table SM.7.1).

Discussion

In this pre-registered diary study, we examined the awe that nonreligious British adults experienced over the summer holidays. Participants distinguished between transformative, amazement, and reverential awe. As predicted, amazement awe was the most frequently reported type and transformative awe the least frequently reported type. The three types differed in their contexts and phenomenology, and most experiences were rated as spiritual but not religious. However, neither the frequency nor the extent of awe predicted changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality from before to after the summer. In exploratory analyses, the amazement rating of participants' most aweinspiring experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing.

Our findings support the distinction between different meanings of awe, extending our previous findings on the semantic associations of amazement and reverence (van Mulukom et al., in preparation) to experiences in daily life. Nature was the most common context for all three types of awe, but beyond this, the types had distinct profiles. Reverential awe was more often related to moral beauty and close ones, which corresponds with the older meaning of awe as deep respect. Transformative awe was more often related to large-scale nature, space, and religious, spiritual, or mystical experiences, and was the most intense type on the awe ladder, the AWE-S, and the ESSS. This is consistent with our proposal that Keltner's (2023) description captures a rarer and more profound form of awe, in which one's understanding of the world is exceeded (see also Gottlieb et al., 2018). Studies that ask participants about awe without specifying its meaning may therefore capture different experiences depending on how participants interpret the word.

Some of our predictions about phenomenology were not supported. Self-diminishment and selfdiffidence were higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences, and reverential awe experiences were rated lowest on the AWE-S and the ESSS. Reverence ratings were also the only awe measure that was not positively correlated with the others, and they were unrelated to how spiritual an experience felt. One possibility is that the meaning of awe in contemporary English is closer to amazement than to reverence, as also suggested by our previous findings (van Mulukom et al., in preparation). Measures of awe such as the AWE-S may therefore primarily capture amazement, and only partially capture reverence. Future research could examine the phenomenology of reverential awe in more detail.

Most awe experiences (90.0%) were rated as not at all religious, but over half of the experiences, and over three-quarters of transformative awe experiences, were rated as at least somewhat spiritual. Spiritual ratings increased with the extent of awe. These findings are in line with previous research showing that nonreligious individuals also report spiritual experiences, particularly in nature (Preston & Shin, 2017), and with the proposal that nonreligious individuals may experience transcendence directed towards this world rather than towards a deity (Coleman et al., 2013). They also suggest that, for nonreligious individuals, the spiritual quality of awe does not depend on a religious framework.

Contrary to our predictions, neither the frequency nor the extent of awe predicted changes in the outcomes over the summer, and the relationship between awe and spiritual yearning did not depend on initial levels of yearning. Pre-summer scores accounted for most of the variance in all outcomes, which suggests that these constructs were relatively stable over the six weeks. Our findings are consistent with those of Monroy et al. (2023), who found that awe was associated with wellbeing at the daily level, but did not predict wellbeing at follow-up. They are also consistent with recent failures to replicate several effects of induced awe, including on life satisfaction (Graziosi et al., 2026). Together, these findings suggest that the longer-term consequences of awe may be smaller or less general than previously assumed.

Across the sample, spiritual yearning and wellbeing decreased slightly from before to after the summer, whereas meaning in life, religiosity, and spirituality did not change. Because the post-summer survey took place at the start of September, these decreases may reflect the end of the holiday period rather than the experiences of the summer, although our design does not allow us to test this.

The exploratory analyses of peak experiences suggest that what matters may be the strength of one's most awe-inspiring experience, rather than the number or average intensity of experiences. The amazement rating of the peak experience predicted higher post-summer meaning in life and wellbeing, whereas its reverence rating and AWE-S subscale scores did not. This is in line with the suggestion of Graziosi et al. (2026) that the intensity of awe may determine whether it has lasting effects. However, these analyses were not pre-registered, and the effects were small, and so they require replication.

Several limitations should be noted. First, our design was correlational, and so we cannot conclude that awe experiences caused any of the observed associations. Second, participants rated only the first-listed, most significant experience of each type in each diary, so the ratings may overrepresent more intense experiences. Third, although the diary design reduced the time between the experiences and their reports, participants still reported experiences retrospectively, and Diary 1 covered a longer period than Diary 2. Fourth, amazement and reverence were each assessed with a single item. Fifth, the six-week period may have been too short for changes in relatively stable constructs such as meaning in life and spirituality, and future studies could follow participants over longer periods. Finally, our sample consisted of nonreligious British adults recruited online. Because religiosity showed a floor effect, we could not examine religiosity as an outcome, and future research could examine whether the same types of awe, and the same associations with spirituality, are found among religious individuals and in other cultural contexts.

In conclusion, awe is felt in a variety of experiences. Nonreligious British adults distinguished between transformative, amazement, and reverential awe in their daily lives, and these types differed in their contexts, intensity, and spiritual quality. Although awe was often experienced as spiritual, its frequency and extent did not predict changes in meaning in life, wellbeing, spiritual yearning, or spirituality over the summer. Future research on the consequences of awe should take into account which type of awe participants experience, and how strong their most awe-inspiring experiences are.

Frequency of the three types of awe

The proportion of participants reporting each type differed significantly in Diary 1, Q(2) = 103.18, p < .001, and Diary 2, Q(2) = 68.49, p < .001, as well as across both diaries, Q(2) = 112.54, p < .001. Holmcorrected McNemar tests showed that all pairwise differences were significant (all ps < .001). Analyses of the full frequency scale (none, once, two to three times, more than three times) showed the same pattern. Frequency differed between types in Diary 1, χ²(2) = 104.20, p < .001, W = .29, and Diary 2, χ²(2) = 70.51, p < .001, W = .19. Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests showed that transformative awe was reported less frequently than amazement awe (Diary 1: r = .66; Diary 2: r = .55) and reverential awe (Diary 1: r = .44; Diary 2: r = .26), and that reverential awe was reported less frequently than amazement awe (Diary 1: r = .41; Diary 2: r = .43; all ps < .001). Finally, how often participants reported the three types was only weakly correlated (Diary 1: ρs = .04-.22; Diary 2: ρs = .08-.34).

Contexts at the participant level

As a sensitivity analysis, each context was counted only once per participant and type of awe. Mind-body practices or hobbies fell below 15 and were added to "Other". The results were similar, χ²(26, N = 519) = 77.58, Monte Carlo p < .001, V = .27. Transformative awe was again over-represented for large-scale nature (z = 2.26), space (z = 3.55) and religious, spiritual or mystical experiences (z = 3.26), and under-represented for close ones (z = -1.99) and witnessing great skill or effort (z = -2.49). Reverential awe was over-represented for moral beauty (z = 4.27) and close ones (z = 2.07), and under-represented for largescale nature (z = -2.27) and space (z = -2.47). Amazement awe was over-represented for mental stimulation (z = 2.02) and under-represented for moral beauty (z = -2.83). The only difference from the event-level analysis was that amazement awe was no longer under-represented for religious, spiritual or mystical experiences (z = -1.75).

Correlations between the awe measures

We pre-registered that the four awe measures (AWE-S, ESSS, awe ladder, and the single-item awe ratings) would be highly correlated within any one experience. Across experiences, AWE-S and ESSS scores were highly correlated (r = .83), and both correlated moderately with the awe ladder and amazement ratings (rs = .46-.50). Reverence ratings correlated weakly with the other measures (rs = .05-.36). Within participants (repeated-measures correlations, df = 174), the AWE-S correlated with the ESSS (r = .71), the awe ladder (r = .55), and amazement ratings (r = .55). The ESSS correlated with the awe ladder (r = .51) and amazement ratings (r = .43; all ps < .001). Reverence ratings were not associated with the AWE-S (r = .02, p = .793), the ESSS (r = .13, p = .084), or the awe ladder (r = .12, p = .111), and were weakly negatively associated with amazement ratings (r = -.18, p = .019).

Religious and spiritual ratings

The ratings were compared in a linear mixed model with rating (religious vs spiritual), type of awe, their interaction and diary entry as fixed effects. Participant and experience were random intercepts.

The random-effects structure was singular. Associations with the awe measures were tested in separate linear mixed models with standardised variables, diary entry as a covariate and a random intercept for participant.

SM.4 Co-experiencers

In an exploratory analysis, we examined who the participants were with during their awe experiences.

Most experiences were shared with others (69.4%): with one other person (36.3%), a small group (25.3%) or a larger group (7.8%). The remaining 30.6% were experienced alone. This distribution differed between types of awe, χ²(6, N = 320) = 13.58, Monte Carlo p = .035, Cramér's V = .15.

Almost half of the transformative awe experiences happened alone (48.9%), compared with 30.9% of amazement and 22.0% of reverential awe experiences (Table SM.4.1).

Experiences shared with others were ranked higher on the awe ladder than experiences had alone (0.23 SD, p = .04), and received lower scores on the AWE-S connectedness subscale (-0.29 SD, p = .012). These models controlled for type of awe and diary entry. Being with others was not associated with AWE-S (p = .73), ESSS (p = .06), amazement ratings (p = .35) or reverence ratings (p = .36).

Change scores

We pre-registered change scores (post-summer minus pre-summer) as an alternative way of testing Adding the amazement and reverence ratings did not improve any model: meaning in life, F(6, 117) = 0.75, p = .61; wellbeing, F(6, 117) = 1.42, p = .21; spiritual yearning, F(6, 117) = 0.62, p = .71; spirituality, F(6, 117) = 1.11, p = .36. In the final models, the only significant individual predictor was the reverence rating of amazement awe experiences, which was associated with an increase in spirituality (β = .27, p = .03); all other ps ≥ .06. Frequency was not associated with change in meaning in life (β = .09, p = .29), wellbeing (β = .03, p = .74), spiritual yearning (β = .17, p = .06) or spirituality (β = .02, p = .86).

Supplementary Materials SM.3 Phenomenology of awe experiences Awe subscales and self-diffidence

We pre-registered the following predictions. Perceived vastness would be higher for amazement than for reverential awe. Self-diminishment and self-diffidence would be higher for reverential than for amazement awe. Connectedness would not differ between the two. Need for accommodation would be highest for transformative awe. The analyses followed the same approach as in the main text (Table S2).

Self-diffidence was computed from ESSS items 14-17 (small, insignificant, self-conscious, irrational emotions). Items 18 (frightened) and 19 (ashamed) were excluded because of low item-rest correlations and floor effects (pooled α = .67; α = .60-.71 across diary entries and types).

Perceived vastness was higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences, F(2, 218.66) = 17.75, p < .001 (0.39 SD, p < .001), as predicted. Need for accommodation differed between types, F(2, 226.29) = 4.32, p = .014. It was higher for transformative than for reverential awe experiences (0.40 SD, p = .011), but not than for amazement awe experiences (0.26 SD, p = .085). Selfdiminishment, F(2, 225.43) = 9.36, p < .001, connectedness, F(2, 224.65) = 6.66, p = .002, and selfdiffidence, F(2, 212.48) = 12.23, p < .001, were higher for amazement than for reverential awe experiences (0.24 SD, p = .013; 0.21 SD, p = .047; and 0.24 SD, p = .005, respectively). Self-diffidence was highest for transformative awe experiences (vs amazement: 0.39 SD, p = .002; vs reverential: 0.64 SD, p < .001). Time perception, F(2, 215.62) = 8.16, p < .001, and physical sensations, F(2, 217.96) = 7.31, p < .001, were both lowest for reverential awe experiences.

, covering altered time perception, self-diminishment, connectedness, vastness, physical sensations, and need for accommodation. Responses ranged from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Very much). Awe. Participants separately rated amazement awe and reverence awe through single items, with a response range from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Very much). Awe ranking. Participants ranked each experience from 0 (No awe, an everyday experience) to 10 (The most awe you have ever experienced). Self-transcendence. Experiences were assessed for self-transcendence with the 19-item Experiential Self-State Scale (van Mulukom, 2026). Responses ranged from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Very much). Experiential religiosity and spirituality. Participants separately rated how religious and spiritual each experience felt through single items, with responses ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Very much).

. Participants rated their feelings over the past week, with responses ranging from 0 (None of the time) to 4 (All of the time). Meaning in life. Meaning in life was assessed using the 15-item Meaning of Life Scale (van Mulukom, in preparation), covering meaning, direction and purpose, coherence, belonging, and significance (see SM.1 for items and factor analyses). Responses ranged from -2 (Strongly disagree) to 2 (Strongly agree). Reliability was excellent (ω = .95 & .96 of pre-and post-measures, respectively). Spiritual yearning. Spiritual yearning was assessed using nine items from the Spiritual Yearning Scale (Wilt et al., 2026), supplemented by four additional items. Responses ranged from -2 (Strongly disagree) to 2 (Strongly agree). Religiosity and spirituality. Participants separately rated their religiosity and spirituality at baseline and follow-up through single items, with responses ranging from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Very much). Procedure Participants completed baseline and follow-up surveys six weeks apart, with two intervening diary surveys at approximately two-week intervals.
